1.tense: Here, with the pen, endings happen because they are ready, not because you pushed them.
1.verb: Letting what's finished actually finish
1.place: In the open, before anything has been chosen
1.ask: Hand half of what you've been carrying alone — a task, a worry, a turn — to someone else, and let their half stay theirs. Then don't count what comes back.
1.core:
Something in you knows when a thing is done, and you act on it without much drama. A job ends, a friendship changes shape, a way of living stops fitting, and you let it go because staying would cost more than leaving. What comes after gets room to arrive because you didn't force it. The endings are clean, the space they leave is open, and you're standing in it without needing to name what fills it yet.

Fairness is the hand that keeps this clean. What you give and what you take stay roughly level, and you don't keep the receipts. Next time someone offers to carry part of what you've been holding, let them. Hand over one piece, keep the exchange even, and notice how much lighter the week goes when the load is shared rather than balanced alone.
1.sheetLine: You end what's finished and trust what comes after.

2.tense: Somewhere ahead of you the next ending is already being arranged, before this chapter has had its say.
2.verb: Letting what's finished actually finish
2.place: In the open, before anything has been chosen
2.ask: When someone close tells you their week has gone badly, stay with them instead of smoothing it over or stepping back. Don't fix anything and don't leave. Just keep talking until they're through.
2.core:
You're good at walking away. You can set down a job, a room, a person, and call it freedom, and sometimes it is. But you release things fast now, and some of them are being let go before they've had a life. A friendship is halfway through a hard season and you've already written it off; a plan hasn't failed yet and you're gone. The openness ahead feels like possibility, and underneath the hurry is something you'd rather not sit in.

Staying is slower than leaving. Next time someone close tells you how things actually are for them, let it hit you before you respond. Don't fix it. Don't reroute. Stay with what they handed over, and say the one thing that moved in you. That contact is what the endings are for — clearing space so something real can arrive, not so you can be gone before it does.
2.sheetLine: You clear the space before anyone can reach you.

3.tense: A door stands closed at your back, and you are still facing it, waiting for it to open.
3.verb: Letting what's finished actually finish
3.place: In the open, before anything has been chosen
3.ask: Take whatever your attention keeps returning to — a person, a project, an old problem — and move one step toward it. Not a plan. One move, before you feel ready.
3.core:
Loyalty is your default, and it has kept good things alive past their season. But something here has stopped being alive, and you keep tending it, calling that faithfulness. A role, an arrangement, a version of yourself you've outgrown — you're holding it steady. The green in you hasn't stopped. It's being spent keeping the old thing standing.

Movement comes first, understanding later. Take whatever your attention keeps returning to and move toward it — a call, a first step, a yes or a no you've been circling. You don't have to know what it means yet. Direction from felt pull is the whole method. Once your energy has somewhere to go, the ending that's already begun stops needing your permission.
3.sheetLine: You're loyal to something that's already gone.

4.tense: Something is ending in you right now, and you have no idea that it is.
4.verb: Letting what's finished actually finish
4.place: In the open, before anything has been chosen
4.ask: Write one thing that feels unsettled — a decision, a situation, your own week — as three lines: what it is, what's changing, what's yours to do. Nothing more.
4.core:
Endings have a way of happening to you without an announcement. Energy drops, a pull goes quiet, and you file it under tired or busy. Meanwhile the old shape is already loosening, and nobody has named it, you included. The quiet isn't emptiness. It's the space after something left, and you're still acting like nothing went.

Putting it on paper is how this becomes yours. Take one unsettled thing and write three lines: what it is, what's shifting, what's yours to actually do. That's it — a container small enough to see into. You don't need to know why things changed. Once the shape is down where you can read it, the ending is something you're doing rather than something being done to you.
4.sheetLine: Something's ending in you and you haven't noticed.

1.tense: You can end a thing here once it has finished being itself.
1.verb: letting what must end end, so the next thing can begin
1.place: where direction gets chosen
1.ask: Take the ending you keep circling and size it honestly — what actually finished, and what's only fear. Say it to yourself at that size, then act from there.
1.core:
Endings reach you as timing, not as loss. When something has finished being itself, you feel the finish and you close it — no dragging it out, no dressing it up — and that is why the next thing arrives when it should instead of late. Closing clean is a skill you already have, and it is why you keep moving on stretches where other people stall. You can say this, not that, and mean it.
The thing to watch is proportion. You can end well and still overshoot, cutting more than the situation asked for because the knife was already out. Before you act, weigh what actually finished against what you're only done with. Close the real thing, and leave the rest alone.
Keeping this balance takes something of you: sitting with the full size of what's going, without letting the size talk you into a smaller cut or a bigger one.
1.sheetLine: You end what's finished, and you end it clean.

2.tense: You will keep ending things before they have had a chance to live.
2.verb: letting what must end end, so the next thing can begin
2.place: where direction gets chosen
2.ask: Before you close the next thing, spend a few minutes with one person and let what they're carrying land on you — no fixing, no verdict, decide nothing that day. What still needs to go will still need to go.
2.core:
Endings have started coming first, with the reason written in afterward. You close a thing before it can fail and call it freedom, and it does feel like freedom for about a day. What's underneath is a knot in the chest about what it might become, and cutting is how you stop finding out. That is not the same movement as clearing.
What you're missing is contact. When you let yourself be reached by what someone next to you is carrying — actually feel it, not think about it — the pressure to cut drops and what's genuinely finished shows itself. Then you can end the dead thing and leave the live one standing. Your own endings get truer when theirs get felt.
2.sheetLine: You end things before they fail, and call it freedom.

3.tense: You were standing at a door that had already closed behind you.
3.verb: letting what must end end, so the next thing can begin
3.place: where direction gets chosen
3.ask: Follow the pull for one hour this week — wherever your attention keeps drifting toward, spend that hour there, and leave the old thing where it sits. No plan, no decision, just the hour.
3.core:
You have stayed at a door that stopped being a door without choosing to stay. The part of you that picks a direction has gone quiet, and the quiet has been read as a verdict — as if the not-choosing settled something. It didn't. Nothing in you is committed to this; you just haven't moved.
Charging straight at it won't work, so don't try to bully yourself into an ending. Follow what's already pulling. Spend an hour where your attention keeps drifting, and the stuck door will show itself as a door and not a wall. The old thing closes behind you once you're walking away from it, and the walking is what you're actually being asked to do.
3.sheetLine: The door shut. You're still parked in front of it.

4.tense: Something in you is finishing and you have not been told, even by yourself.
4.verb: letting what must end end, so the next thing can begin
4.place: where direction gets chosen
4.ask: Put three unedited lines on paper — what was, what is, what you'd pick. No ending required. A small container you can read when you want to.
4.core:
You are steering from a place you haven't consulted about a change already underway. Something has been finishing in you, and you have been navigating this stretch as if the floor were still the same floor. Nothing about this calls for drama. It calls for being told — and you are the one who gets to find out first, because the knowledge is already in you, just not in your hands.
Build the smallest thing that holds it. Three lines is enough. Pattern isn't control; it's a container you can carry, and once the mess has a shape you can read where you actually stand. Then you can choose with it instead of around it.
4.sheetLine: A change is already underway and you haven't heard about it.

1.tense: Endings are arriving by felt necessity right now, and the renewal behind them is being trusted.
1.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive
1.place: at the still point where what matters shows itself before you can say why
1.ask: Find an arrangement where the two sides have drifted — a cost, a standing favor, a recurring effort — set it level once, then keep your hands off it and see whether it holds.
1.core:
Things are finishing around you because they are finished, not because you cut them off, and that is why the clearing feels clean instead of sharp. You can sense in a thing whether it has run its course, and you move on that sense rather than on the calendar or on someone else's timeline. What comes after the ending is already arriving.

That same even eye works on exchanges. Where a share has drifted, you feel the tilt before you sit down to figure it out. Test it on something small: a household split, a favor you keep covering, an effort that keeps landing on one side. Set the balance right, once, honestly, and then stop adjusting. The point is the proportion you leave standing, not a habit of correcting.
1.sheetLine: You can tell what is finished, and you let it finish.

2.tense: Before this ending has taught you anything, the next one will already be declared.
2.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive
2.place: at the still point where what matters shows itself before you can say why
2.ask: Before you call the next ending, spend ten minutes with someone who is in the middle of their own change, and offer no advice, no reasons, no fix — just stay with what they are carrying.
2.core:
You are clearing faster than things can finish. A situation gets heavy, an exit appears, and taking it feels like honesty. From where you sit it reads as freedom; from where those near you sit, the furniture keeps moving. The next ending is often chosen before the current one has taught you what it had to teach.

What is missing is not less change, it is contact. Sitting with someone who is also mid-change, and not managing their process, brings you back near the floor. Their upheaval is no threat to your judgment, and you do not have to solve it. Feeling it alongside them — while keeping your own feet — is what tells you whether this ending is real or rehearsed.
2.sheetLine: You are calling endings before they have lived.

3.tense: That door closed already, and you are still standing in the doorway, loyal to the room behind.
3.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive
3.place: at the still point where what matters shows itself before you can say why
3.ask: Choose something you want that the old arrangement cannot give you, take a step toward it today — a call, a signup, a message out — and wait until after the step to decide what it means.
3.core:
Something was over before you noticed, and you keep it running anyway. Holding it takes most of what you have, so from inside it looks like care and from outside it reads as loyalty. The old shape is the room you live in. What has not happened is a single move toward whatever comes next, because the last thing has not been set down.

Your direction runs on feeling, and the feeling still points at the old room. So the repair is not a verdict about what should end — it is a small step toward something you actually want. One move, today, before you have settled whether you mean it. The step itself shows you where your energy is willing to go, which is more reliable than any conclusion you could reach about the past.
3.sheetLine: You are loyal to something that has already ended.

4.tense: An ending is underway right now, and nothing in your week has a label on it yet.
4.verb: letting what has finished end, so what is next can arrive
4.place: at the still point where what matters shows itself before you can say why
4.ask: Take the topic you keep drifting back to lately and give it a shape outside your head — a few lines on a page, a folder, dates — so it sits somewhere you can see it instead of inside you.
4.core:
Something is at the end of its run, and it is finishing without your hand on it. You might notice the tiredness, a subject that keeps returning, a flatness in something you used to look forward to. None of it has been named as change, so nothing has been made ready. The sense of what matters is there, and it has nowhere to sit.

Build one small container. Take the thing you keep circling — a role, a tie, a decision — and give it a form outside: a page, a folder, a handful of lines with dates. You are the one who made it, and it can sit out there from now on. What is coming apart is already telling you its name; you are only giving that a place to be kept.
4.sheetLine: Something is ending and you have not named it.

1.tense: Right now the ending is here and you are standing in it without flinching.
1.verb: ending what has finished so what is next can begin
1.place: where what is growing is tended without being forced
1.ask: This week, when you give something — an hour, a hand, a meal — let something come back, and don't hand it away at the door.
1.core: You can tell the difference between something finished and something merely hard, and you act on it. What ends, ends because it is done, not because it failed, and you don't drag the old shape behind you into what comes next. People feel it in the way you care — steady, unhurried, no grip. The give and take in that care tends to run one direction more than you'd choose. Checking on what you tend, taking a hand when it's offered, letting a meal be cooked for you — small returns. That's not keeping score. It's what keeps the care from running dry. Try it once this week and see what shifts.
1.sheetLine: You can tell what's finished, and you let it finish.

2.tense: You will be braced for the next rupture before the present one has even settled.
2.verb: ending what has finished so what is next can begin
2.place: where what is growing is tended without being forced
2.ask: Stay with whoever is carrying something heavy, in it, for a while, and fix nothing.
2.core: You can see the ending coming, and you can see it everywhere. Something gets clear enough to be finished and you finish it before it's lived, and the release seems like gain while it lasts. There is real ending in you, and it has started arriving ahead of what it belongs to. The way through starts with whoever is across from you. The mess and the person need company, not a rescue committee. Sit with them in it a while; don't tidy it, don't hand them a cleaner version. Stay in your own seat while you do. If they ask what you see, then you can say it.
2.sheetLine: The ending is arriving before the thing it belongs to has finished.

3.tense: You were standing at that door long after it had already closed behind you.
3.verb: ending what has finished so what is next can begin
3.place: where what is growing is tended without being forced
3.ask: Follow a pull you already feel — somewhere, someone, some direction — and go a little way toward it.
3.core: You keep something alive past the point where it can grow. There's loyalty in that — to a person, a role, a version of things — and it's holding you at an address you've already left. Not because you can't end things. Because ending feels like the wrong answer, so you keep watering what's already gone. What moves you out isn't a reckoning. It's motion in whatever direction something in you is already leaning. The pull is the direction; it doesn't have to be large or reasoned. Take a step before it's tidy, before the last piece is in place. The ending happens on the way, not before it.
3.sheetLine: You keep watering something that's already finished growing.

4.tense: Something in you is finishing right now and you have not yet put it into words.
4.verb: ending what has finished so what is next can begin
4.place: where what is growing is tended without being forced
4.ask: Give what you're carrying a container — a time, a room, a place it lives.
4.core: You are good at caring for what's growing — steady, patient, no forcing. And you haven't looked at what's ending, or that anything is. The ending is real and unnamed, and the care is aimed elsewhere. What brings it into view is a small structure. Not a reckoning — one container. A time on the calendar, one room for the thing, one hour set aside for what's actually going on in you. The mess doesn't have to be solved; it has to be given walls. Put it somewhere you'll see it. That's not making a decision. That's making the decision visible when it's ready.
4.sheetLine: The ending is happening and you haven't looked at it yet.

1.tense: Right now an ending arrives from something you can feel, not something you've argued yourself into.
1.verb: Ending what has finished so what's next can start
1.place: Where pattern gets built and a mess gets a usable order
1.ask: Hand back a load someone could carry themselves, and take back what of yours is sitting with them. Then leave the ledger alone.
1.core:
Where you build order, an ending lands clean when it's time and needed. You can tell the difference between something that's finished and something you're tired of, and you don't need a case built to act. When a structure has done its work, you close it without turning the close into a judgment on anyone.

Past that, giving and receiving has to run both directions or it stops being either. There's likely a load you've been carrying for another person that they could carry themselves, and something of yours resting with someone else. Hand the first back. Take the second back. What's fair moves between you and doesn't need to be entered anywhere. The evening after, there's nothing to check.
1.sheetLine: You end what's finished, and you don't have to keep the receipts.

2.tense: The next thing you end will be ended before it has had its life.
2.verb: Ending what has finished so what's next can start
2.place: Where pattern gets built and a mess gets a usable order
2.ask: Stay with the arrangement you're three steps from clearing — answer the message, keep the hour, don't close it. If it's finished, it'll wait. Call someone first if that helps.
2.core:
You build order well, and when that runs hot, the building turns into clearing the room ahead of anyone arriving. Something gets ended before it has had its life, and it's your call, made for the relief it brings. From outside, the ground keeps moving under the people in it.

Going somewhere hard with a thing, and staying while it's hard, is the way back. Pick something you're three steps from ending — a plan, an arrangement with a person — and stay with it longer than you'd otherwise. Answer the message. Keep the hour. Don't tidy it. If it really is finished, it will still be finished later. Often the room didn't need clearing. It needed you in it.
2.sheetLine: You end things fast, and the relief does not last the week.

3.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already shut behind you.
3.verb: Ending what has finished so what's next can start
3.place: Where pattern gets built and a mess gets a usable order
3.ask: Some arrangement at work or home has stopped moving and you're holding it up. Take one visible step — a call, a box, a message that says this part is done — then stop.
3.core:
Where you build order, little is being built just now, because a shape that was true once has stayed standing past its time and you keep holding it. Calling that loyalty doesn't change it: a structure still going that has already stopped, and no end has arrived to let what's next start.

Feeling ready isn't the door. One move is. Take a single step with the arrangement that has stopped — a phone call, a box out the door, a message naming the part that's finished. Then stop, so your hands learn there's an after. The energy you have goes into that direction, not into holding the old shape up. The next step shows itself once this one is done.
3.sheetLine: You've been keeping something alive that has already stopped.

4.tense: Something is already ending in your week, and if asked you'd call the week ordinary.
4.verb: Ending what has finished so what's next can start
4.place: Where pattern gets built and a mess gets a usable order
4.ask: Give a line and a date to whatever is shifting for you — a person, a commitment, a season of work. What you do with the page is yours.
4.core:
You keep the shape of things — a container here, a rule there — and most of it is happening under the surface. Right now something is changing, the change is already underway, and you'd say nothing much was going on. The writing is happening. You haven't looked at what it says.

Give the change a container and it becomes visible: a line and a date on what's shifting — a person you see less, a commitment running out, a season of work closing. You aren't deciding anything on paper. You're reading the page you're already writing. Whatever is ending becomes an ending you know about, and what to do next week gets easier to see.
4.sheetLine: An ending is already underway here, underneath the week.

1.tense: You are here, at the end that is finally happening, and it is going through.
1.verb: Letting what is finished finish so what is next can begin
1.place: In closeness where two people feel the same thing and keep their own sides
1.ask: With the person nearest what's ending, keep giving what's yours and taking what's offered — both directions, no tally at the close.
1.core:
The closeness you're in runs both directions, and it's carrying an ending with it. Something is finishing out in the open. You aren't dragging it past the place it already ended, and you aren't going numb to dodge the goodbye. That is why the people near you can stay near you while it happens — nobody is being asked to hold a door shut.

What you have already is proportion by feel: you give what's yours, you take what's offered, nothing counted. The growth part is to keep that moving out loud — tell one person what is ending and what you need after. Then trust the exchange to keep flowing without a record of it. The feeling moves through instead of pooling.
1.sheetLine: What's ending is finishing cleanly, and you're still here for it.

2.tense: You will keep ending things before they've had a chance to end on their own.
2.verb: Letting what is finished finish so what is next can begin
2.place: In closeness where two people feel the same thing and keep their own sides
2.ask: A bond you were about to close this month — stay in contact across the next hard stretch, not fixing anything and not walking out. Let what's carried reach you; hold your own ground in it.
2.core:
Endings are easy to feel coming, and lately they arrive early. Close it first, before it can go somewhere outside your control — the ending feels like freedom, but the clearing is outrunning what actually needed to end. Anyone watching can tell the exit is being rehearsed.

You don't have to read the outcome. Stay in contact while it's hard — one bond you were ready to sever, one difficult stretch, this month. Sit in it without fixing anything and without leaving. Let what the other person carries reach you, and hold your own ground in it. If the end comes, let it come from what's real rather than from getting ahead of it.
2.sheetLine: The ending is coming early because you're running it.

3.tense: You kept something alive past its end and called it loyalty.
3.verb: Letting what is finished finish so what is next can begin
3.place: In closeness where two people feel the same thing and keep their own sides
3.ask: Follow one pull you already feel toward something new — a place, a person, a first step — and give today's hours to that direction instead of the finished thing.
3.core:
Someone or something is finished and you are still at its door. Your time, your worry, your staying keep going back there, and it's already gone. Loyalty is the name you've given it. The real thing is that no ending gets to happen near you at all, and your closeness sits constant while the thing it's attached to is past.

The way out isn't a feeling you're waiting on. Go where the pull already is — one direction you genuinely want, one step taken today, before you feel ready. Being done with the old thing first isn't the price; the step is what lets the door close. The desire you already carry does the work once your energy stops going backward.
3.sheetLine: What's dead is still holding your days.

4.tense: Something is ending in you and you have not looked at it.
4.verb: Letting what is finished finish so what is next can begin
4.place: In closeness where two people feel the same thing and keep their own sides
4.ask: Give what has finished in you the smallest shape that holds it — a time, a place, the next move, set down together. A container, not a verdict.
4.core:
Something has stopped and you keep moving as if it hasn't. You don't know what it is — a role, a hope, the shape a closeness used to have — and not knowing keeps it open. There's no story about it you'd recognize, because you haven't given it one.

You can stop there. Build the smallest thing that holds it: set the ending down along with when and where you'll meet it, and the next move. Not a verdict on the bond, not a decision only you can make — a container. Once the ending has a shape you can carry it instead of it carrying you. What you couldn't see becomes something you've held once, and it starts to move.
4.sheetLine: You don't know what's finished in you yet.

1.tense: Right here, with the pen, this has run its course and you are letting it close.
1.verb: let what is finished finish and turn the cleared ground toward the goal
1.place: on the road toward the thing you are after, between one work and the next
1.ask: Pick an exchange you're in the middle of with someone. Make it a straight swap — what you give matched by what you get — and keep no tally of who owes whom after.
1.core:
The ending and the push run on the same fairness here: you hand back what this was owed, the goal gets clear road, and the exchange keeps moving without a ledger in your hands. That is how it stays clean. Something that lived gets set down, whoever was in it gets what their part earned, and the road toward what's next opens. Nobody has to come up short for the closing to happen. Fairness and finishing are one motion, and both keep moving.
There's a person or a piece you'd wait on if you could. Settle that part first — take your half out, pay what your share owes, hand theirs back to them. Some of what you're moving toward gets asked about before the clearing finishes, and you'll answer cleaner with the books straight. Let the first settlement show you what the movement feels like when nothing is outstanding. What it costs to keep an exchange even, you already pay gladly.
1.sheetLine: You let a thing finish and keep the road clear after it.

2.tense: You are already braced for the next ending before this one has had its life.
2.verb: let what is finished finish and turn the cleared ground toward the goal
2.place: on the road toward the thing you are after, between one work and the next
2.ask: Choose someone with a stake in whether this survives. Say what the ending looks like from where you stand, then stop talking and let their whole week reach you, not just the part about this.
2.core:
You can feel a thing ending before it has finished, and you've started clearing ground before the actual close. Your year reads as a string of fresh starts, each one up fast, each one already braced for the next break. From outside it looks like freedom. From inside it's the fear of what happens if something runs all the way to its natural end around you. Nothing gets to live long enough to prove it's safe.
Not every ending needs clearing yet. Some still have their own length to run. Sit with one person who's in this with you, without trying to fix what they feel, and stay in contact while it's hard — you keep your own side, they keep theirs, and you're still there through the middle. That last part hasn't happened yet, and it's the one that would tell you whether the ending you keep reaching for is real.
2.sheetLine: You end things early so nothing can end on you.

3.tense: You are still standing where this went through a long while back.
3.verb: let what is finished finish and turn the cleared ground toward the goal
3.place: on the road toward the thing you are after, between one work and the next
3.ask: Take one step toward what you actually want — an email, a call, a single sentence sent — and do it before you feel like it, not after.
3.core:
You're pointed at something, and you aren't arriving. Something already closed, and part of you still keeps the shape it had: the same course, the same losses, and the name you have for it is staying true. Nothing new gets a beginning because the old thing hasn't been released. Loyalty to what's over can pass for patience, and it isn't. It's the same movement, stalled, one street back.
Let the feeling pull, then move with it. Something in you is already heading somewhere, even if you won't give it that name. Send the smallest next piece today — a sentence, a call — before you're ready, because the readiness may not show up first. The step is what carries you through. You don't have to see the destination from where you're standing. You just have to be further than this morning.
3.sheetLine: You are loyal to something that already ended.

4.tense: Something is already over, and you are steering the whole goal around it unnamed.
4.verb: let what is finished finish and turn the cleared ground toward the goal
4.place: on the road toward the thing you are after, between one work and the next
4.ask: Take the tangled part of this you don't look at much. Put it into one shape on paper — what's in it, what's closed, what's still open, a line each — then read it once.
4.core:
You keep steering around something this goal already ended, and you haven't named it. The direction is measured against a thing that isn't there anymore, and the gap doesn't show. It stays out of view because naming it would mean a chapter that closes, and the structure you run on doesn't have that page yet. Everything else in the push gets a plan.
Put a shape around the mess and look at it once. One page: what's in it, what's over, what's still live, a line each. Not a decision, not the ending — just the thing made small enough to carry. The act is the structure itself, not the answer it produces. What you're doing is giving the direction somewhere to stand, so the goal can run from what's actually present instead of from something you haven't looked at. You don't have to end it to see it plainly. Seeing it is the whole ask.
4.sheetLine: The goal is steered around something already over.

1.tense: Right now you are letting something end because it has finished, not out of avoidance.
1.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
1.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure
1.ask: If you're settling something with someone, adjust the share until it's fair — give back what's owed you both. Then stop, and don't revisit it to check.
1.core:
Endings you trust come from the centre here, and you can tell the difference between something that's done and something that hurts. What has finished gets honoured rather than propped up. You're able to say out loud that a thing is over without turning it into a punishment for anyone, least of all yourself.

To keep that, offer one exchange the shape it actually has. If you're settling something with someone, adjust the share until it's fair — give back what's owed you both. Then stop, and don't revisit it to check. It may be an apology owed, or time, or the last word. The balance holds because you stop when it's level, not because you keep score. Let the fair thing rest once it's fair.
1.sheetLine: You end what has finished without turning it into punishment.

2.tense: You will be reading the next release as liberation before anyone has lived inside what is ending now.
2.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
2.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure
2.ask: Pick one hard thing you're in and stay with it — the person it touches, or the fact itself. Don't end or fix anything yet.
2.core:
Endings come fast here, and each one looks like freedom before it has been lived through. An upheaval starts to feel like growth, and the fear underneath gets called release. What's actually needed is the opposite of more clearing: staying in the thing long enough to find out what it is.

So instead of cutting, remain. Pick one hard thing you're in and stay with it — the person it touches, or the fact itself. Don't end or fix anything yet. Contact that outlasts the discomfort is what tells you whether the ending is real or only wanted. Some of it will settle by itself; the part that stays will tell you what it is. The choice will be yours without the hurry.
2.sheetLine: You call fear liberation and end what hasn't finished.

3.tense: You keep holding what ended a while back, and you call the holding loyalty.
3.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
3.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure
3.ask: Find one place your attention is already drawn, and put an hour into moving it one step — a call, a box, a message, a page. One step only.
3.core:
Here you carry what you've carried a while, and some of it has been over for longer than you'd say. Holding on reads as faithfulness, so nothing gets cleared, and the strength that could bear a real ending keeps bearing a finished one instead. The stagnation looks like loyalty from where you stand, and from outside it looks like standing still.

Don't try to want the ending. Go where the pull already is. Find one place your attention is already drawn, and put an hour into moving it one step — a call, a box, a message, a page. One step only. Momentum comes from the feeling you do have, not from summoning one you don't. The step tells you more than a decision would.
3.sheetLine: You stand at a door that closed a while back.

4.tense: Something is already ending around you, and you carry it without knowing you are.
4.verb: Honouring necessary endings and letting what has finished clear
4.place: Where you bear what must be borne, and hold form under pressure
4.ask: Write five lines about what is changing near you, worded as what happens next, not what you feel. The last line is what you do about it this month.
4.core:
Changes are underway close to you, and the bending happens quietly: you attend to the day without noticing that a chapter has already turned. The strength that holds things steady is doing its work, and what it holds is partly gone. Most of the people near you can see it before you can. What you are carrying is real; you are simply the last to know it.

Give it a shape on paper, because shapes reach you where feelings don't. Write five lines about what is changing near you, worded as what happens next, not what you feel. The last line is what you do about it this month. Reading it back, you may find you already knew, and now it has somewhere to stand. Nothing has to be decided tonight; the page will keep it.
4.sheetLine: Something is ending near you and you carry it unaware.

1.tense: Right now, something has run its course and the leaving of it is already underway.
1.verb: ending what has finished so what comes next can start
1.place: the daily practice kept by repetition, where the small steady light is tended
1.ask: Let your practice move both ways this week — help offered, help taken — without keeping count of either.
1.core:
You can end a thing when it has actually ended. That is a rarer skill than starting one. Where you keep your practice, you notice what has finished, you let it finish, and you don't drag the husk along with you. Because you go by what you feel rather than what you fear, the cleanup is quiet and usually right-sized.

What keeps this clean is that it stays even. Some of what moves is given out, some is let in, and both directions stay open. An uneven exchange, even a generous one, wears a person down slowly, and your practice is the first place you would feel that. Keep both ways open and the ending stays easy to do.
1.sheetLine: You end what has ended, and the next thing has room.

2.tense: Somewhere ahead, endings are already being lined up and rehearsed before anything has finished living.
2.verb: ending what has finished so what comes next can start
2.place: the daily practice kept by repetition, where the small steady light is tended
2.ask: Stay in contact with the difficult thing one week past where you would usually cut it — one more session, one more unhurried conversation — before deciding anything.
2.core:
Out ahead of yourself, endings happen early. Things get cleared before they have lived, and that reads as liberation right up until you notice how much you keep having to clear. That is the shape of it: motion that looks like release and is really bracing, because the next loss is already being prepared for.

Staying is the plainer move. Not forever — a week past where you would usually go. Stay in contact with the difficult thing while it is still hard, without fixing it or yourself. Whatever is actually finished will still be finished after the week. Whatever is not will tell you so, in a way you can feel rather than decide.
2.sheetLine: You end things early, so nothing gets to prove itself.

3.tense: A door is behind you now and your hand has not moved off it.
3.verb: ending what has finished so what comes next can start
3.place: the daily practice kept by repetition, where the small steady light is tended
3.ask: Follow the pull that is already there — a step in a direction that has been tugging at you, small enough that getting it wrong costs nothing.
3.core:
Where you practice, everything is kept exactly as it was. The motions are the same ones, repeated, and repetition has quietly become preservation. Nothing here is being refined toward anything anymore; it is being kept alive by habit. That steadiness is real, and from inside it, it doesn't feel like fear. Whether it is loyalty or stalling, you are the one who would know.

Momentum moves through the practice. Follow a pull that is already there, before you feel ready — a direction that has been tugging at you, small enough that getting it wrong costs nothing. Effort aimed straight at the stuck place won't do it. What is finished can rest once something else has your feet, and something already does.
3.sheetLine: You are tending something that finished, and calling it loyalty.

4.tense: You are already letting something go, and you would not say so if asked.
4.verb: ending what has finished so what comes next can start
4.place: the daily practice kept by repetition, where the small steady light is tended
4.ask: Build the smallest shape around it — a start, a stop, an order — and set that where you will see it. No fixing, no one told.
4.core:
Somewhere in you, something is ending, and the ending is happening without your hand on it. You practice, and the practice holds. Whatever is passing is not being marked as passing. From the outside, others can likely see it; from yours, this is simply how things are, and there is nothing to report.

Naming it changes nothing about the ending, only about who is doing it. Build the smallest shape around it — a start, a stop, an order — and set that where you will see it. No fixing, and no one has to be told. Once it has a shape, the leaving is something you are choosing rather than something landing on you, which is the difference between being carried and walking.
4.sheetLine: What is leaving you is leaving, and you didn't say so.

1.tense: Endings are moving through you by consent, and nothing is being torn out.
1.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
1.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in
1.ask: Give a finished thing a real goodbye — a thank-you, a returned key, a last honest word. Then take back what you're owed, today.
1.core:
Things are closing around you, and you're letting them close. Not because you're stoic about loss, but because you can feel when something has said what it came to say, and you'd rather see it off than keep it breathing on a machine. That's why what's arriving has somewhere to land — you keep clearing space without making a scene of the clearing. The leaving and the coming in are the same motion.

The part worth your attention now is the trade. When something ends, something also comes back to you: an hour, a room, an honest answer you'd stopped expecting. Say that out loud once this week. Hand back whatever you're holding that isn't yours, and take what is. The next thing at the door needs the room, and it needs you to be the one who calls the balance fair.
1.sheetLine: You can end a thing and still take back what it owed you.

2.tense: You will cut this loose before it has had a chance to be itself.
2.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
2.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in
2.ask: When the urge to call something over arrives, sit with whoever else is in it before you decide. Feel what they carry. Then choose.
2.core:
There's a way of moving on that is really just leaving early. You can feel the pull to close a role, a plan, the shape of a relationship, and the closing wears the face of freedom. It isn't. It's what staying long enough to be changed would cost, paid up in advance so you don't have to find out.

Stay in contact a bit past when the impulse speaks. When you want to call it finished, sit with the person or the situation first — let what they're carrying reach you, and keep your side while it does. You can feel someone without becoming them. And then, if it's still finished, close it. You'll be ending something real instead of something feared, and that's the whole difference. Only you can tell which one you're holding.
2.sheetLine: Not every ending is freedom. Some are just leaving early.

3.tense: A finished thing still has your weight on it, and you are leaning there.
3.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
3.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in
3.ask: Take a step away from something that's over — a call, a box, a road you keep retaking — ahead of feeling ready. Today, not later.
3.core:
You've been keeping faith with something past its life. The faithfulness is real; it's aimed at the wrong thing. What's over doesn't need a guard, and leaning on its door spends the room the new thing would use. Stepping away isn't the same as saying it mattered less.

The way forward opens from motion first and feeling later. Go where something in you is already leaning, even a little, and trust the rest to show up once you've gone. Put energy you actually have into the direction you'd pick if the choice were free today. Direction doesn't arrive as certainty; it arrives as motion you can keep. Small and today beats whole and someday.
3.sheetLine: Leaning on a finished door isn't loyalty. It's just still waiting.

4.tense: Something is already ending in you, and it goes unnamed.
4.verb: ending what is finished so the new can arrive
4.place: the threshold where what was outside comes in
4.ask: Set down on one page what is actually leaving your life right now — plainly, nothing rearranged. That page is the container.
4.core:
Something in you is rearranging, and it has been arriving as tiredness, or a busy stretch, or nothing in particular. You've been carrying the change around without knowing you were. Nothing's being hidden on purpose — the thing simply hasn't been put into a shape, so it moves through the days unnamed and spends you sideways.

Give it a container small enough to lift. One page, one list, one line — whatever is actually ending, set down flatly, with nothing tidied up. You don't have to act on any of it. The point is to move the thing out from under the description you've been using for it, so you're holding it rather than it holding the day. You'll know it's worked when the mess has an edge, and the edge is one you drew.
4.sheetLine: You're carrying a change that hasn't been written down yet.

1.tense: What has ended for you is being let end, and the next thing is already being trusted.
1.verb: ending what has finished so the new thing can start
1.place: at the table where the shares are weighed and set right
1.ask: With someone you trade with — favors, rides, dinners — let the next one run its whole length untracked. Give without noting the balance, or take without squaring it afterward.
1.core:
Some things have ended under your hands, and you're letting them stay ended. You can feel when something is finished, and you don't take it back for comfort or reopen it for a second pass. The clearing happens at a pace that isn't yours to hurry, and you trust it.

What comes next you let arrive rather than hauling it forward. That's rarer than it sounds. People see a door close and read it as a loss that has to be repaid. In your accounts it just closes.

So let one exchange run full length with someone you trade with — give without marking it, or take without squaring it afterward. One person, one exchange, nothing added. If the share lands uneven, sit with it rather than adjusting it the same day. You don't need the ledger here.
1.sheetLine: What's finished, you let stay finished — even when no one says so.

2.tense: Something is ending in your hands before it has had any life to spend.
2.verb: ending what has finished so the new thing can start
2.place: at the table where the shares are weighed and set right
2.ask: At a moment this week when someone near you is carrying something heavy, let it land on you before you answer. Don't resolve it, don't fix it, don't leave the room.
2.core:
Something is ending in your hands before it has lived. This project, this arrangement, this version of yourself — you're past each one before it has begun, and the rush feels like bravery. It isn't. The clearing that used to follow your sense of what's finished has become a standing policy, and things are being cut while they're green.

Deeper down something is being shed already; there's just no room to tell what should go next. What waits to be reached is what you've been moving too fast to touch.

At one heavy moment, let someone's load land on you before you answer — don't clear it, don't leave. And before you close the next thing, keep it running a week beyond where you'd have stopped it. See what it looks like still alive.
2.sheetLine: Things are ending in your hands while they're still green.

3.tense: A door closed some time back, and you have not moved from the spot where it stood.
3.verb: ending what has finished so the new thing can start
3.place: at the table where the shares are weighed and set right
3.ask: Give an afternoon to whatever already has a pull on you — a person, a room, a piece of work — and follow it without deciding anything about the rest.
3.core:
A door closed some time back and you're at the spot where it stood. You've been calling that loyalty. It might be — but nothing waits on the other side of it, and the days keep going by. What used to feel like holding on has turned into a way of not moving at all.

The share is out of true: you keep giving to something that's already over, and taking nothing back.

There's a pull in you somewhere. Follow it for an afternoon — a person, a room, a piece of work — and give it your whole attention. Notice where your energy actually wants to go. Nothing has to be settled about the old thing today; one afternoon, one direction, that's all.
3.sheetLine: You're at a door that closed a while back.

4.tense: Something is ending in you and the ending has not been given a name.
4.verb: ending what has finished so the new thing can start
4.place: at the table where the shares are weighed and set right
4.ask: Make a container for one confusing area of your life — a folder, a labeled box, a dated page. You don't have to fix what's in it, just make it hold.
4.core:
Something is on its way out in you and it hasn't been written down. Not because you're hiding it — you just haven't looked directly, and the not-looking carries its own momentum. From the inside it feels like nothing is happening. From where others stand, you've been moving on for a while.

When this season does get named, it goes easier. The container comes first; the feelings catch up.

So make one for a messy area of your life — a folder, a labeled box, a dated page on the calendar. You don't have to fix the thing or understand it. You only have to make it possible to hold. What's ending will still be ending after, and the container is what carries it.
4.sheetLine: Something in you is ending and hasn't been named yet.

1.tense: You are here in the middle of it, and endings are arriving on their own schedule.
1.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
1.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you
1.ask: Between you and someone, a favour or a running tab has been kept square. Let it drift this week without tracking the return. No clock on it. Set the ledger down and see.
1.core:
Something in your life is already finishing, and you can feel that it is. You're not fighting it and you're not rushing it — you're letting it take the time it takes, and you're still around while it does. That's rarer than it sounds, and it's what makes the next thing possible rather than just hoped for.

When a thing ends, you don't need to know what fills the space. The clearing is the point. So let one exchange go loose. There's a place between you and someone where you've kept the books even — a favour given, a favour owed. Drop it for now. Not forever, not as a rule. Long enough to feel what happens when you're not holding the scale. Fairness that flows finds its own level without a hand on it. That's the part you're trusting, and you can afford to.
1.sheetLine: You let things finish, and you stay around while they do.

2.tense: You will be braced for the next thing to end before it has even begun to live.
2.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
2.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you
2.ask: Next time you feel the pull to end something early — a plan, a project, a tie — don't decide yet. Stay near it through one more hard stretch. Not fixing it. Just not gone from it.
2.core:
You're ending things ahead of their time. Not because they're finished, but because finishing them early feels like freedom, and waiting feels like a trap. It isn't. The upheaval looks like liberation from the outside and feels like bracing from where you sit — you're already three endings past where you actually are.

Courage isn't the gap. Company is. Something is being carried near you — a person, a situation, a piece of work — and you're managing it from a distance instead of standing next to it. Stay close through the hard part. Not fixing, not deciding, not ending. Just staying. The true ending will still be there when it's true. The ones you jump to now are the ones you'll be finishing again later, and twice is worse than once.
2.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've had a chance to be.

3.tense: You were still at a door that closed behind you a long while ago.
3.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
3.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you
3.ask: Something you want is already pulling at you. Follow it one step today, in the direction your body already leans. No plan, no permission, no announcement to anyone.
3.core:
Something in your life finished a while back and you've kept it standing. You tell yourself it's loyalty, or patience, or being the kind of person who doesn't walk away. It might be all of those. It's also a weight you're carrying because putting it down would mean it really ended, and ending is the thing you've been avoiding for longer than you'd say plainly.

The way out isn't a bigger push. It's a smaller one, in a direction you already have. There's something you want that you haven't moved toward — not a project, just a pull. Go where that pull is, one step, today. You don't need to feel ready. You don't need to know what you're releasing. The movement does the clearing. Holding still doesn't hold anything; it keeps you in a room you already left.
3.sheetLine: You're holding something up that already finished its life.

4.tense: Something is ending in you right now, and you have no words for it yet.
4.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
4.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you
4.ask: Take whatever has been taking up room — a plan, a habit, a commitment — and give it edges: a date it's done, a place it stops. Once it has a shape, leave it be.
4.core:
You can't name what's shifting. Something in you is letting go and the part of you that writes things down hasn't caught up. You'll feel it as fog, or flatness, or a low hum of something you can't place — and you'll treat it as a problem to solve rather than a change already underway.

You don't have to know what it is. Give it a container anyway. Take whatever has been taking up room — a plan, a habit, a commitment you keep half-holding — and put an edge on it: a date it's done, a place it stops. The shape makes it visible. Visible, you can work with it. The ending was going to happen whether or not you named it. Naming it just means you get to be there for it.
4.sheetLine: Something is ending in you, and you haven't met it yet.

1.tense: You are here with the pen, and what's finished is being let finish.
1.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
1.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started
1.ask: Pick a swap with someone that has drifted out of kilter — you carrying more, or giving less than is fair. Say what each side puts in, out loud, then land on a single trade you can both keep from here.
1.core:
A shared thing has done its work with you, and you can tell. A habit of feeling, a way you and another person have done it since before you can remember — when it's done, you release it, and you trust what comes after. The people close to you can feel that what you let go is let go cleanly, not dropped on them.

So work the next one aloud. Take an exchange that has drifted out of proportion and say what you're owed and what you owe in the same breath. Hear the other side. Land on a fair swap you can both keep, then stop counting. That is how the ends you make stop feeling like verdicts — they become trades, kept loosely, and the room after them is one nobody has to defend.
1.sheetLine: You can let a shared thing end without it becoming a loss.

3.tense: You were standing at a door that closed behind you a season ago.
3.verb: letting what is finished end, so what comes next can begin
3.place: at the threshold where the old thing is done and the new one hasn't started
3.ask: Take the smallest real step toward a direction that still pulls you — make the call, sign up, walk over — and take it before the day ends, while the old slot still sits on your calendar.
3.core:
Something you cared about is over and you're still keeping its place warm. The date you go through, the habit you rehearse, the person you wait to hear from — the event has finished and you haven't finished attending it. That keeping is loyal, and it is quietly costing you the hours something alive would use.

You don't have to kill it. Move a wanted thing into the slot the finished one still occupies, and go there instead. One real step in a direction that still pulls you, taken today, before the old slot gets filled by another week of waiting. What's over ends by being replaced, not by being buried, and you don't owe anyone an announcement. Doors close when you simply walk through a different one.
3.sheetLine: It's over. You've been going on keeping it.

1.tense: The letting go has its shape now and your hands are steady in it.
1.verb: Letting what has finished finish, so what is arriving can arrive
1.place: In the adjustment itself — adding here, subtracting there, hands on the balance while it moves
1.ask: Take what is being handed back — the rest, the help, the credit — and keep it, with no return gesture ready.
1.core:
You are past the part where you decide whether to let this finish. The date exists. Your attention goes to keeping the hours honest — the last message, the things to hand over, the loose account — and because your grip is loose, the ending keeps handing back parts of yourself you did not know were out on loan. That is not a reward, it is what a clean ending returns. The position holds without you.

Still, balance is an active thing, so keep one adjustment going. Take your own share for granted: something small, yours by right, taken without flinching and with nothing owed in return. Then the ending is an exchange rather than a bill you quietly pay alone.
1.sheetLine: What is finishing is doing it with your full attention on it.

2.tense: Every door still swinging toward its first day gets shoved shut by you before the week is out.
2.verb: Letting what has finished finish, so what is arriving can arrive
2.place: In the adjustment itself — adding here, subtracting there, hands on the balance while it moves
2.ask: Stay a conversation past the point where you would normally end it — not to fix anything, just to remain where it is hard.
2.core:
You are ending things ahead of their own pace. Plans get abandoned while they are still warm — nothing has failed, you have just found a wall before it had a chance to be a wall — and every clearing feels like freedom until the next one is needed, sooner each time. That is what makes the clearing tiring rather than clean.

One draw is marked for you. Stay in something a little past your quitting point, a conversation you would normally walk out on or put a wall across. Not forever, just past the hard part. Staying close to what is difficult, without your hand on the exit, is the practice that teaches your timing where the real edge is — and lets you find out how much of the ending was honest.
2.sheetLine: You are closing things that haven't finished happening.

3.tense: A room that emptied is still being kept tidy by you.
3.verb: Letting what has finished finish, so what is arriving can arrive
3.place: In the adjustment itself — adding here, subtracting there, hands on the balance while it moves
3.ask: Follow the pull you already feel past the point of thinking about it — walk toward it, and keep walking until that has decided.
3.core:
There is a room in your life that emptied, and you still tend it. You are loyal to something that has stopped answering, and you set that down as steady; the effort of keeping it going is slow but it is not idle, and it uses time that has nowhere else to go. That is not a character flaw. It is a person standing at a threshold, deciding whether to cross.

The thing that would pull you across is not a grand ending; it is a direction — any one with an actual pull on you. Follow whatever already draws a little of your energy, past the point of only thinking about it. Direction is not decided, it is met, and the walking starts the rest.
3.sheetLine: You are tending something that has already stopped answering.

4.tense: A page turned weeks ago has not been noticed by the one who turned it.
4.verb: Letting what has finished finish, so what is arriving can arrive
4.place: In the adjustment itself — adding here, subtracting there, hands on the balance while it moves
4.ask: Write out, from memory, the order of what changed recently in your life, and keep the page.
4.core:
You have already let some things end. The problem is you have not been told, least of all by yourself — you keep handling what is left as though the arrangement were temporary. That is one of the ways a change this deep goes missing: nobody hands you a receipt, and the next task is more pressing than noticing.

So make the change visible. Write out the order of what happened, from memory, in plain steps, as an instruction to someone in your shoes. It is quick, and it forces the ending to exist somewhere outside you. Most of these pages take ten minutes and change nothing except the fact that the ending has been seen.
4.sheetLine: Something in your life has already ended and you haven't been told.

1.tense: You are here at the completion, and you are letting it finish.
1.verb: ending what is finished so the next thing can begin
1.place: where you see the shape of things without their contents
1.ask: Name what you gave in something that has finished, and name what came back. Add the two up out loud if that helps. Once the scales read even, set them down and leave them.
1.core:
You can watch something end without rushing it or holding it back. What's finished gets to be finished, and what's next doesn't have to be named yet. You know when a thing has run its course, and you act on that instead of waiting for someone to hand you a reason.

Exchange is what keeps an ending clean for you. You give what the closing asks and take what's yours from it without holding a running tally past the point where the two sides match. This week, take stock of one finished thing — what went out, what came in — and when the count levels, put it down. You'll notice the pattern underneath sooner once the balancing isn't running in the background.
1.sheetLine: The ending stays clean while give and take stay level.

2.tense: You are bracing for a change you can't write yet, so you end things first.
2.verb: ending what is finished so the next thing can begin
2.place: where you see the shape of things without their contents
2.ask: Before you cut the next thing loose, sit with someone it touches and feel what they're carrying without losing your own footing. Stay there a while. Decide nothing yet.
2.core:
You're clearing things before they've had their season. A friendship, a role, a plan — when it gets tense, you end it, and the ending feels like freedom. It isn't quite. It's the relief of not having to wait for something you can't control, and the relief is what you're chasing, not the ending itself.

The pattern you're good at seeing has gone thin: you're reading the shape of what's coming more than what's actually here. Sit with somebody this touches and feel their side without dissolving into it. You don't have to keep the thing. You just have to stop ending it alone.
2.sheetLine: You end things early so the future can't end them for you.

3.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
3.verb: ending what is finished so the next thing can begin
3.place: where you see the shape of things without their contents
3.ask: Something wants you and you've been slow to answer. Take a step toward it today — send the message, make the call, look it up. One step only, then stop.
3.core:
Something in your life has already ended, and you're still tending it. You give it names — loyalty, patience, not being the kind of person who walks away — and the names hold it upright. From the outside it looks like standing very still in a room that's already been emptied.

A pull in you points somewhere else. You can feel the direction without having said it. Follow that one step today. Not because the old thing was wrong, and not to prove anything. Because the part of you that knows what it wants is the part that knows when something's over, and it hasn't been consulted.
3.sheetLine: You're loyal to something that's already gone.

4.tense: You are writing the next chapter without noticing that the last one ended.
4.verb: ending what is finished so the next thing can begin
4.place: where you see the shape of things without their contents
4.ask: Take a foggy stretch of your life and set down a single rule for it — what comes first, what's over, what you stop doing. One line, one page, kept where you'll see it.
4.core:
You rearrange your life constantly and call it normal. People leave, jobs shift, plans change, and you've already moved the furniture before anyone asked whether you noticed. The pattern-sense is strong: you see how things fit together. What you don't see is that a few of the pieces you keep fitting were for a shape you've outgrown.

Give that stretch one rule it can live by — a line about what comes first or what you've stopped doing. It won't fix the fog, and it isn't meant to. It puts the ending somewhere other than a feeling you keep stepping around. The shape you draw is the one you go by.
4.sheetLine: You've been rearranging a room that's already changed shape.

1.tense: You are here now with the pen, and what has run its course is being set down complete.
1.verb: ends what is finished so what is next can start
1.place: where a false structure is coming down all at once
1.ask: Take one exchange you have been keeping even, and let a turn of it pass without a tally — a favor given, or an owed back taken — then leave the count alone for good.
1.core:
When something between you is out of balance, you feel it and set it right without doing arithmetic. Nothing gets ruled on for being a feeling; nothing tips the scale. You weigh it, adjust it, then stop. That is what fair recognition looks like in your hands, and it is rare.

The ground under it is less steady than the fairness makes it seem. What has ended between you and someone else lands right only when you can leave it alone before every corner is even. Give one exchange back its natural two-way flow, and keep the accounting off it. Part of you would rather hold the ledger at zero. Give and take moving freely will teach you more than the ledger ever did.
1.sheetLine: You can feel through it and name what is fair.

2.tense: Somewhere ahead of you a structure is coming down before it has had time to stand.
2.verb: ends what is finished so what is next can start
2.place: where a false structure is coming down all at once
2.ask: Next time something between you starts to crack, stay in the conversation past where you would usually call it done — long past the first wave. Keep contact going, not a verdict on whether the thing should continue.
2.core:
You can feel what is ending in you early, and the ending gets decided before anything has had a life. A structure that isn't finished is already being closed, and from where you stand it looks like liberation. From the other side of the table it looks like something leaving before its time.

What is missing is not more endings. Stay in contact with the person or the thing just past where it gets uncomfortable, and let what is between you be felt rather than finished. You don't have to fix it or agree with it. You don't have to stop deciding. Just stay past the point where you normally go, and notice what is still there when you do. The pace of the ending will change once the contact does.
2.sheetLine: You end it before it's had a chance to live.

3.tense: You are still at a door that has already closed behind you.
3.verb: ends what is finished so what is next can start
3.place: where a false structure is coming down all at once
3.ask: Name what you actually want — say it plainly, nobody else has to hear — then move toward it today, before the day gets away. Not the safe version. The one you already lean toward.
3.core:
What is done is done, and you are parked at it, calling that loyalty. The door has not moved; you have stopped. Something in your life is already finished, and staying looks like fidelity from the inside. From the outside it looks like a wait that no longer has anything to wait for.

Forward motion is still in you — it is just not being spent. Move toward something you actually want, today, while the feeling is real. Not the whole plan. A step small enough that you can't fail it. Direction comes back by being used. A step taken today does more than a year standing at that door, and it does not need your permission to be the right one.
3.sheetLine: You're still at a door that closed behind you.

4.tense: Something in you is ending right now and the pen has not been picked up to set it down.
4.verb: ends what is finished so what is next can start
4.place: where a false structure is coming down all at once
4.ask: Take something already shifting in your life and give it the smallest shape that could hold it — a container, a date, a place. Nothing has to change yet. Put it where you can see it.
4.core:
Something in your life is already ending, and the part of you carrying it has not been told. What is closing feels like climate — you are inside it, not doing it. The ending moves through your week as mood, as fatigue, as an itch you can't place, and nothing gets named.

Name a single piece. Take the thing that is already shifting and give it a container small enough to set on a table: a date, a place, a sentence saying what is closing. You don't have to act on it. You don't have to decide anything. You put the shape where you can see it — and the part of you doing the ending stops being a stranger, because now there is something on paper that says what they were doing.
4.sheetLine: Something in you is ending and hasn't been told.

1.tense: The thing under your hands is coming to its end, and it is being let come.
1.verb: letting what's finished come to its end so something else can take its place
1.place: where what you actually want is still just a bearing, not a road
1.ask: Look at the ending under your hands and who is carrying what around it — move a part so it sits fairly, then leave it alone.
1.core:
You can let something finish in the open. You feel what's done and you don't hold it, so the space it leaves gets used, and your sense of the next thing stays a real bearing rather than a wish.

After an ending you have one pull worth guarding: to even out who carried what. Once. Take the thing that's closing and see who was left holding which part; move one piece so the weight squares, then let the rest be. Do it again and the ending turns into a ledger and the bearing goes dim. This isn't indifference — it's settling the account in a single motion and letting the account be settled.
1.sheetLine: You let a finished thing end, and even the share once.

2.tense: You will end this before it has run, and the next ending is already being chosen.
2.verb: letting what's finished come to its end so something else can take its place
2.place: where what you actually want is still just a bearing, not a road
2.ask: Name the next thing you're pulling the plug on — then stay near whoever is most inside it this week, and don't wrap it up for them.
2.core:
Where you steer by what you want, endings get declared before the thing has lived, and each is spoken of as liberation. Underneath is bracing: get the loss behind you first so it can't be given to you. The clearing stops being something you feel and starts being something you do to whatever might end by itself.

Contact is what reopens this. Take the next ending you were about to announce and stay with the people inside it for a week instead of closing it early. Sit in the middle with them and don't rush them out the other side. A farewell you declared in advance is a flinch wearing its coat; one that comes after you've stayed is finished.
2.sheetLine: You end things early and name it freedom — the bracing shows.

3.tense: You were at that ending some time back, and the doorway is where you remain.
3.verb: letting what's finished come to its end so something else can take its place
3.place: where what you actually want is still just a bearing, not a road
3.ask: Begin a thing you want today without waiting to feel settled — the first move, made now, not the mood around it.
3.core:
The pull toward what you want is intact. What hasn't moved is the ending that would let you follow it. Something finished is where you left it, and holding it looks like loyalty. The draw toward light stays a bearing instead of a road, and nothing new gets the room.

Direction comes through a step, not through deciding. Pick the smallest move toward something you actually want — a message, a visit, a first piece of the thing you keep describing — and take it today, before you feel certain. One real move does more than a season of holding. The ending doesn't need to be performed. It can just be left where it is, in the rear, while you walk.
3.sheetLine: You kept a finished thing standing, and the new road has no room.

4.tense: Something is ending in you at this moment, and it has not been named or noticed.
4.verb: letting what's finished come to its end so something else can take its place
4.place: where what you actually want is still just a bearing, not a road
4.ask: Take what's shifting in you and set down the order it goes in — what ends, what stays, what comes after.
4.core:
You've been steering by a light you hadn't pointed at, and something has been finishing underneath the whole time. Nothing in you has marked it, so the change goes on unnamed, and you describe your direction as a given rather than a choice you keep making.

Put the order down. Take what's shifting and lay out what ends, what stays, what comes after. A scrap of paper will do, or a date and a place attached to it. This doesn't decide anything early or close a door. It lets you see which ending is underway, so your sense of the next thing stops being a hunch and starts being a bearing you chose.
4.sheetLine: Something's ending under you — set down the order it goes in.

1.tense: The ending is happening at the right time, and it is being done cleanly.
1.verb: ending what's finished, so the new thing has room
1.place: in thick fog where each step is lit only as you take it
1.ask: Where you'd normally hand back exactly what you were handed, receive one kindness without settling it, and pass one along without watching for the return. No ledger, no deadline.
1.core:
An ending is underway in your life and you're doing it well. You can feel when something has finished — not by argument, by a sense of what can't go on — and you've let it end without dragging out a farewell or turning it into a fight. What's coming next isn't clear, and you're fine with the fog. When a step shows itself you take it, and the taken steps have been landing true.

The fairness you keep in all this is part of why it holds. Where you've been living by handing back exactly what you're handed, be a little looser. Take one kindness without counting it and return one without waiting to be repaid, so the exchange moves in both directions without you holding it. It keeps the new thing fed while the shape of it is still forming.
1.sheetLine: The ending is yours, and you're doing it clean.

2.tense: You will keep being the one who clears the room, and the clearing keeps outrunning the life.
2.verb: ending what's finished, so the new thing has room
2.place: in thick fog where each step is lit only as you take it
2.ask: When the urge to end something arrives, don't act on it that day. Stay beside whoever it touches and let what they carry reach you, without agreeing with them or taking their position as your own.
2.core:
The clearing has picked up speed. Things get ended here before they've had a life — a plan, a situation, a way of working — and each ending gets called freedom, though it arrives right before you'd have to try. You're braced a season ahead, shutting things down so they can't disappoint you first. The fog isn't the trouble; you're moving too fast for it to matter what's actually there.

What's missing is someone else's reality next to yours. Before the next ending, sit with whoever it touches and feel how it looks from where they sit, without merging into it or talking them out of it. You can leave after. The difference is whether you left knowing what you left.
2.sheetLine: The clearing has outrun the life it was clearing.

3.tense: You were standing at a door that closed behind you, and you are still standing there.
3.verb: ending what's finished, so the new thing has room
3.place: in thick fog where each step is lit only as you take it
3.ask: Notice which direction something in you keeps tugging toward, and follow it once — a call, a place, an hour spent on it — before you've worked out whether it's sensible.
3.core:
Something in your life has already ended and you're treating it as ongoing. You keep the routines, the care, the showing up, long after whatever it was stopped being alive, and calling that loyalty is the kindest name for it. The fog has been an excuse here — no clear path, so none taken — and still days pass in which nothing moves toward anything you'd choose.

Nothing gets cleared by waiting. Notice which way something in you is already leaning, and follow that lean once, before you've decided it's sensible or found the whole route. The fog doesn't lift first; the step is what lights the next stretch. What you're keeping doesn't need another month of you. What's next does need the step.
3.sheetLine: You keep a thing that's finished. It doesn't keep you.

4.tense: Something has been ending here, and you are still writing as if it has not.
4.verb: ending what's finished, so the new thing has room
4.place: in thick fog where each step is lit only as you take it
4.ask: Take one page and set down the order your days actually run in — what comes first, what follows, what you'd keep if you had to choose. Written plainly, no verdict on any of it.
4.core:
An ending is underway in your life and it hasn't reached your account of things. You keep planning on ground that is quietly shifting, and someone who asks how it's going gets the version from before. The fog gets blamed for the uncertainty, but the uncertainty sits downstream of something you haven't put a word to yet. That's all that's missing — a word, not the ending.

Give what's here a container. One page holding the order your days actually run in — what comes first, what follows, what you'd keep if the choice were forced — so the shape is written down rather than carried silently. You don't have to decide anything from it. Once it's on the page, what has been ending usually says so.
4.sheetLine: Something is ending, and your account hasn't caught up.

1.tense: The endings arrive when they are due, and you trust what comes after them.
1.verb: ending what has finished, so what is next can begin
1.place: where what you are becomes visible by what you let end
